fields.Front: Name the three levels of the three-schema architecture and say what each describes.
fields.Back:
1. External level: the external schemas or VIEWS - each shows only the data one user or program cares about and hides the rest.
2. Conceptual level: the structure of the whole database for all users, normally described as tables (the relational model); this is where you build in this course.
3. Internal (physical) level: physical storage - the hard disks, the ones and zeros, and the INDICES that give fast access.

fields.Front: Give the instructor's weather-database example of two external views, and her hospital example.
fields.Back: Weather: a web program that needs only Ontario data and a mobile app that needs all of Canada - each program is shown only the tables and data it needs. Hospital: a nurse's view might show patients and rooms but not billing.

fields.Front: Define logical and physical data independence and say what each protects.
fields.Back:
Logical data independence: the capacity to change the CONCEPTUAL schema without affecting the EXTERNAL schemas/views - it protects the views and programs from new or changed tables.
Physical data independence: the ability to change the INTERNAL schema without changing the CONCEPTUAL schema - it protects the tables from changes in storage.
The goal is to have both.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: a failing disk is replaced and an index is built on OHIP number. Which level changed, which independence applies, and who notices?
fields.Back: The internal (physical) level. Physical data independence applies. Designers do not change their schema and programmers do not change code; the only thing anyone may notice is that access is suddenly a lot faster.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: classify each change by level - (a) add a column to Room, (b) build an index, (c) the Ontario web app now wants Quebec data too.
fields.Back:
(a) Conceptual - logical data independence protects the existing views.
(b) Internal - physical data independence protects the conceptual schema.
(c) External only - just that one view changes; no independence is needed.
Also: adding Prince Edward Island tables to the weather database is a CONCEPTUAL change, and the Ontario-only application 'shouldn't even know' - logical data independence. Caveat: removing a table the application actually uses could still break it.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §2.1.1): name the four categories of data model, with an example of each.
fields.Back:
1. HIGH-LEVEL or CONCEPTUAL: concepts close to how users perceive data - entities, attributes, relationships. The ER and EER models.
2. REPRESENTATIONAL or IMPLEMENTATION, also called RECORD-BASED: understandable to users but close to how data is stored and directly implementable. The relational model, and the LEGACY network and hierarchical models.
3. LOW-LEVEL or PHYSICAL: record formats, record orderings and ACCESS PATHS such as indexing and hashing; meant for specialists.
4. SELF-DESCRIBING: the description of the data is combined with the values. XML, key-value stores and NOSQL systems.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §2.3.1): name the four DBMS languages and what each defines, then define host language, data sublanguage and query language.
fields.Back:
DDL (data definition language): the conceptual schema, and in most systems the external schemas too. Used by the DBA and designers.
SDL (storage definition language): the internal schema. Most relational DBMSs have no separate SDL; SQL's was removed, and storage is controlled by functions and parameters.
VDL (view definition language): external schemas and their mappings to the conceptual schema; SQL plays this role in relational systems.
DML (data manipulation language): retrieval, insertion, deletion and modification. A HIGH-LEVEL/NONPROCEDURAL DML is SET-AT-A-TIME and DECLARATIVE (SQL); a LOW-LEVEL/PROCEDURAL DML is RECORD-AT-A-TIME and needs loops.
When a DML is embedded in a general-purpose language, that language is the HOST LANGUAGE and the DML is the DATA SUBLANGUAGE. A high-level DML used interactively on its own is a QUERY LANGUAGE. SQL is DDL, VDL and DML in one.

fields.Text: We want BOTH kinds of data independence because it makes life easier for the {{c1::DBA}}, the {{c1::designer}}, the {{c1::programmer}} and the end user: a change at one level does not 'screw up' the other person's level.

The three-schema (ANSI/SPARC) levels are {{c1::external}} (views - an Ontario-only web app versus an all-Canada mobile app), {{c1::conceptual}} (the whole database as tables) and {{c1::internal/physical}} (disks, ones and zeros, indices).

Textbook (Elmasri §2.2.2): data independence works because when a schema changes at one level, the schema above is untouched and only the {{c1::mapping}} between the two levels changes. {{c1::Logical}} data independence is the harder of the two to achieve, because it must absorb {{c1::structural and constraint changes}} without touching application programs.
